title: Microrelease SDK Accelerator — Heuristic Manifest
content:
Purpose and intent:
This is a compact operational playbook for shipping tiny, frequent SDK updates (microreleases) with low cognitive overhead for product teams and minimal customer disruption. Focus is on repeatable heuristics: preflight checks, smoke tests, lightweight telemetry probes, and an explicit 15-minute oncall ritual for first-ship visibility.

Why microreleases?
- Faster feedback on API ergonomics and bugfixes.
- Smaller rollback surface and easier bisect.
- Enables rapid experiments on usage/defaults and documentation wording.

Goals (success criteria for a microrelease):
1) No customer-facing errors > P99 over first 24 hours for flows previously exercised by CI.
2) Telemetry pipeline reports stable or improving SDK usage signals within 30m of rollout.
3) If failure, automated rollback completed within 10–20 minutes without data loss.

Quick glossary:
- microrelease: a release with a single user-facing change (bugfix, docstring, telemetry marker) shipped independently.
- smoke probe: a minimal scenario that must pass post-deploy.
- probe owner: person responsible for watching a specific probe for 1st-hour.

Preflight checklist (local + CI):
- [ ] Unit tests pass locally and on CI (run: yarn test:unit or pytest -k 'sdk').
- [ ] Integration smoke harness runs (examples/smoke/*) and returns expected output (sample command: ./tools/smoke-run --target=js --model=redwood-medium).
- [ ] Telemetry tags present in change (sdk.event=... and version tag).
- [ ] Changelog entry (one-paragraph) added to CHANGELOG.md.
- [ ] Minimum rollout plan drafted in PR description (canary %, timeline, who to call).
- [ ] Feature flags used for behavior toggles (if applicable) and default off.

Canary rollout heuristic (opinionated):
- Canary stage 1: internal canaries (10% of internal beta orgs) for 15 minutes. If green, go to stage 2.
- Canary stage 2: progressive 1h ramp to 25% of free-tier sandbox traffic. Monitor P50/P95/P99 and error rates.
- Canary stage 3: full rollout if no regression for 60 minutes; otherwise rollback.

Minimum telemetry probes to create for every microrelease:
- sdk.init.latency: distribution of SDK initialization time (client-side).
- sdk.request.error_rate: grouped by error code and route.
- sdk.default-response-assert: boolean probe for smoke test check.
- sdk.version.usage: counter tagged by sdk_version and language.
- retain a tiny sampling of raw responses (redact PII) for first 2 hours of rollout for one failing scenario.

Smoke tests (fast, deterministic):
- JS quickstart smoke: import client -> init with test key -> call echo prompt -> assert contains marker "microrelease-ok".
- Python embedder smoke: generate embedding for 'redwood-test' and assert vector length matches model profile.
- CLI: run redwood-cli --version and redwood-cli sample-run --expect-ok.

Sample JS smoke script (kept intentionally tiny):
const { Redwood } = require('@redwood/sdk');
(async () => {
  const c = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.RW_SMOKE_KEY });
  const res = await c.chat.create({ messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'smoke probe microrelease-ok' }] });
  if (!res.choices?.[0]?.message?.content?.includes('microrelease-ok')) process.exit(2);
  process.exit(0);
})();

Oncall 15-minute ritual (first 60m post-rollout):
- t+0: Deploy completes -> ping #dx-oncall with release id and canary %.
- t+5: Probe owners confirm smoke probes green or report link to failing run.
- t+15: If any critical probe failing, escalate to release engineer and trigger rollback (see rollback recipe).
- t+60: Confirm telemetry aggregation (sdk.version.usage) and finalize full rollout.

Rollback recipe (fast path):
1) Revert canary routing (automated via platform: reroute command in infra console).
2) Re-deploy previous tag if routing-only rollback insufficient.
3) Add a blocking feature-flag or kill-switch if bug is behavioral and surfaced by new code path.
4) Post-mortem stub: 1-page timeline + root cause and follow-ups within 48 hours.

Observability notes (what to look for in Console):
- sudden spike in sdk.request.error_rate (threshold: >3x baseline and >0.1% absolute increase).
- tail latency (P99) regression > 2x baseline in first 30m.
- new version usage shows expected progression (counts increase) and sampling of text asserts fail.

Lightweight QA matrix (who owns quick checks):
- Docs / copy: Priya Kapoor — verify code snippet updates render in docs site and quickstart playground.
- JS SDK owner: Ethan Park — run JS smoke and check telemetry tags.
- Python SDK owner: Marco Ruiz — run embedder smoke and CI wheels.

Developer-facing quickstart notes to include in every microrelease PR:
- One-line summary of behavioral change.
- Minimal example showing the new behavior (3–7 lines).
- Backwards compatibility notes (what breaks, what doesn't).
- Migration hints and rollout guidance for integrators.

Known tradeoffs and heuristics (copied into PR checklist):
- Keep releases small: if change touches >3 modules, prefer a normal release with wider test window.
- Telemetry must be lightweight: avoid high-cardinality tags in early microreleases.
- Sampling: prefer 10% raw-response capture for 2 hours rather than full capture.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we automate the smoke-run inside the infra deploy pipeline so canary gating is enforced? (RDW-2378 exploring this.)
- Decider: What is the exact error-rate threshold that should auto-block rollout? Current heuristic above is conservative; need SRE signoff.
- UX: Add a one-click ‘abort microrelease’ button in Console tied to rollback recipe.

Next steps (nearterm):
- Wireup sample smoke scripts into repo tools/smoke-runner (owner: Ethan).
- Add sdk.init.latency to telemetry schema and nightly dashboards (owner: Marco).
- Run a dry-run microrelease in staging next week with the cross-team oncall present.

Notes-to-self / rough ideas:
- Consider pairing microrelease approvals with a single thumbs-up scope in PR for small teams (fast path).
- Could we include an optional ‘sample prompt set’ in PR description to exercise likely user flows? Might be helpful for prompt-sensitive regressions.
- Keep the manifest as a living doc; prefer short, actionable lines rather than long essays.

Appendix: quick git commands for revert
- git revert -m 1 <merge-commit> && git push && trigger-deploy previous-tag

End of manifest — feedback welcome.
